headline: China lands a rocket booster on a ship at sea

sources.title: Making history! China lands rocket during an orbital launch for 1st time ever
China becomes second country to recover orbital booster with Long March 10B
China Successfully Launches, Retrieves Reusable Rocket Booster
China catches Long March-10B booster in reusable rocket breakthrough (video, CGTN)

chunks.text: China has {{pulled off}} [[a major step]] in space travel. From the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, a new rocket called the Long March-10B {{took off}}, carried a [[satellite]] into [[orbit]], and then [[guided]] its huge lower part, or [[booster]], [[safely]] back to Earth. China became only the second country, after the United States, to [[recover]] an orbital rocket so it can be used again.

verbs.wrong: To try something for the first time
verbs.correct: To succeed in doing something difficult
verbs.why: A team pulls off an upset win against a much stronger rival, and a chef can pull off a difficult dish under pressure. China pulled off catching its rocket booster in a giant net at sea.

verbs.wrong: To separate suddenly from another part
verbs.correct: To leave the ground and begin to fly
verbs.why: A plane takes off once the runway is clear, and a flock of birds can take off all at once. The Long March-10B took off, carried a satellite into orbit, and later returned its booster safely.

chunks.text: After the rocket climbed high into the sky, its first [[stage]] [[separated]] and {{came down}} toward the sea. About six minutes later, a giant net on a floating [[platform]] caught it. Chinese [[engineers]] had {{set up}} this net capture system, and they had never {{tried out}} such a design in a real flight before.

verbs.correct: To move down toward a lower place
verbs.why: Rain comes down hard during a summer storm, and an elevator comes down to the lobby in seconds. After separating from the rocket, the first stage came down toward the ocean, right where a net was waiting.

verbs.wrong: To repair a machine that had broken
verbs.correct: To create or establish something new
verbs.why: A new business sets up a website before opening its doors, and a scientist sets up an experiment step by step. Chinese engineers set up a huge net capture system that had never been tested in a real flight.

verbs.correct: To test something to see if it works
verbs.why: A shopper tries out a new mattress in the store, and a driver can try out a car before buying it. Engineers had never tried out this exact net design in an actual flight before this launch.

chunks.text: Landing a booster is difficult, but it {{pays off}}. [[Normally]], rockets are used only once and then {{thrown away}}. If the same booster can fly [[again and again]], companies can {{cut down}} their costs and launch [[far more]] often. [[For years]], the American company SpaceX has led this [[field]], and China is now [[working hard]] to {{catch up}}.

verbs.correct: To bring a good result after effort
verbs.why: Months of practice pay off on race day, and extra studying can pay off on a hard exam. Landing a booster is difficult, but for China this attempt clearly paid off with a successful catch.

verbs.wrong: To keep something for the next launch
verbs.correct: To remove something you do not want
verbs.why: People throw away old newspapers after cleaning a garage, and a cook throws away food that has gone bad. Normally, rockets are used only once and then thrown away, but a reusable booster changes that completely.

verbs.wrong: To share costs with other companies
verbs.correct: To reduce the amount of something
verbs.why: A family cuts down spending before a big trip, and a runner can cut down her race time with training. If a booster can fly again and again, companies can cut down their launch costs significantly.

verbs.correct: To reach the same level as someone ahead
verbs.why: A student catches up on missed homework after being sick, and a smaller company can catch up to a market leader. SpaceX has led reusable rockets for years, and China is now working hard to catch up.

chunks.text: The Long March-10B stands about 63 meters tall, and [[one day]] it may help {{carry out}} China's plan to send [[astronauts]] to the Moon. Engineers now want to {{look over}} the returned booster, and they hope to fly it again [[before the end of]] the year. If everything {{goes ahead}} [[as planned]], [[reusable]] Chinese rockets could soon become normal.

verbs.wrong: To announce a plan to the whole world
verbs.correct: To do or complete a planned task or action
verbs.why: Soldiers carry out orders during a drill, and a team carries out a plan step by step. This same rocket may one day help carry out China's mission to send astronauts to the Moon.

verbs.wrong: To repair something before using it again
verbs.correct: To examine or check something carefully
verbs.why: A mechanic looks over an engine before a long drive, and a judge looks over each project at a science fair. Engineers now want to look over the returned booster before deciding if it can fly again.

verbs.correct: To happen or continue as planned
verbs.why: A wedding can go ahead even with rain, and a meeting goes ahead as scheduled despite one absence. If everything goes ahead as planned, reusable Chinese rockets could soon become completely normal.

mainIdea.s: China's new rocket carried a satellite into orbit, and engineers used a net on a ship to catch its booster. This makes China only the second country to recover one.
mainIdea.why: China recovered the booster with a net system, becoming only the second country to recover an orbital booster.

mainIdea.s: China's rocket landing shows the country has caught up with SpaceX and now leads the world in reusable rockets. Engineers plan to reuse the booster many times.
mainIdea.why: Close, but China has not caught up yet. The article says SpaceX has led the field for years.

mainIdea.s: Last year, China sent a new crew of astronauts to its space station for a six-month mission. Officials said the crew would carry out several experiments there.
mainIdea.why: This describes a crew mission to China's space station. The article is about landing a reusable rocket booster on a ship.

tf.s: The Long March-10B took off and carried a satellite into orbit.
tf.why: Take off means to leave the ground and begin to fly, which the rocket did before releasing its satellite.

tf.s: China has already caught up with SpaceX and now leads the field.
tf.why: SpaceX has led for years, so China is still trying to catch up, not leading.

tf.s: After separating, the booster was thrown away into the ocean.
tf.why: The booster was caught in a net to be used again, so it was not thrown away, which means to get rid of something.

tf.s: Engineers said the landing had failed and did not pay off.
tf.why: The landing succeeded, so the effort did pay off, which means to bring a good result.

tf.s: Reusing boosters could help companies cut down their costs.
tf.why: Cut down means to reduce, and flying the same booster again cuts down launch costs.

tf.s: Chinese engineers set up a net system to catch the booster.
tf.why: Set up means to create or establish something new, which is what the engineers did with the net system.
